afternoon, everybody. It is 4:00 PM on September 17th, 2026, and I call the September meeting of the Student Services Committee to order. We'll begin with public comment. Is there any public comment this evening? Seeing none, all in favor of approving the minutes of the August 20th, 2026 Student Services Committee meeting, please say aye. Aye. Aye. That motion has passed unanimously. item number five, which are information items tonight. We'll begin with item 5.01, which is the revised Policy 8140 on student attendance requirements and procedures, and presenting that item tonight is Jennifer Evans, our director of Student Mental Health Services. Well, hello there. Thank you for having me. There were just a few updates through legislation that we want to incorporate into

8140. House Bill 653 provides that excused absences for visitation of immediate family members who are connected with deployment in the military. So if you look on line 59, you'll see the paragraph that we added.

So basically, it says it goes from what it was previously, which was just military obligations, to really laying out that they can have a week with their family member to meet the requirements. And then just in, we received some additional suggestions from legal, just about aligning this with other policies while we are making changes just to reorder it.

So have the definitions at the top, excused and unexcused, and then also separating a section for additional activities and situations that principals can consider, and then maintaining the military obligation as that separate factor for an excused absence. There was another change that was recommended by Jennifer, which was related to civic duties.

We need to change that to allow for up to five absences, and right now it reads as one. So what we were hoping is that if you approved the red on the previous slide, we could also make these changes that were recommended from legal to move it forward as an action item. Committee members, is there any discussion on these revisions? Ms. Lavelle.

Thank you, and thank you for the presentation. I found it very interesting to read this policy this afternoon, and ultimately, I just had some foundational questions. I wanted to note, I did find it interesting, the specific carve-out for 4-H activities. Mm-hmm. And imagine that's been part of the policy for some time now. Oh, since it was adopted in the '70s.

But I was interested to see that truancy is defined as one or more. Is that a legal term? Because when I looked in the code, it wasn't easy to find. So I was hoping that you could explain that a little bit more. Yes. And then speak to how it works, because I have noticed, especially at the beginning of the year, it's not unusual for students to get labeled as truant when really it's the percentage of days that they've missed because there haven't been that many days.

So if you could speak to that, that would be helpful. Yeah. So truancy is absences that the parent is not aware of or supportive of. That the others are unexcused absences that are locally defined, meaning the parent has provided a rationale, but we're determining that it's unexcused based on our policy. But it is based on the number of days. We don't take action until we have five unexcused absences, and that's when we

would develop our plan, and that's all laid out in our regulation, all of the steps that we have to take per the state requirements. And then after seven absences that are unexcused, that's when we move to a multidisciplinary team meeting with the family and the school team. And then from there, if there's continued absences, then we would move towards the court considerations, and our attendance officers might get involved. But most of our absences are

excused absences, as you know from our chronic absenteeism reports that we've done. But truancy really is that intentional not coming to school. Parents don't know where their kids are. So we don't see that all that often. Okay, so you mentioned five and seven. Was it 10 that triggered the- Yeah. -action? So it's five for the plan. Seven is usually when we start looking at whether we need to schedule, if there's a consistent pattern.

But we need to have the conference within 10 days after the 10th absence. Okay. That's how the code's written. Fascinating. Mm-hmm. Okay. Thank you. You're welcome. Ms. Lavelle. Thank you. So it could be actually up to 20 days before anything is actually done, correct? No. I mean, you've got the plan, but it has to be implemented within 10 days following.

Yeah. So the plan, just to clarify, is we can do that between the three and five absences if we're starting to see a pattern. Sometimes it's a family that's taken a trip, and they've told us. So we don't necessarily take that and make a plan, but we just acknowledge that your student's already been identified as chronically absent. We really don't want to see this happen throughout the year with repeat vacations. But at five, there's a written plan that the parent has to be part of, the student

has to be part of developing. What is getting in the way if there are barriers? And then from there, we monitor it closely. Then we will follow up with that seven to 10-day window where it's a larger team conversation, and then from there, that's when the attendance officer will come in. So we try to do everything we can at the school level before. But yes, you're accurate. We could wait till 20 days to have a conference, depending on the availability, but there's constant communication with the family,

emails going, phone calls, home visits on occasion, too. Okay. Thank you. You're welcome. Okay. Thank you. Do you recommend knowing that there's this kind of parent notification understanding with truancy? Because I would envision there are actually maybe times the parent does know the kid is truant and just isn't doing anything about it.

Do you recommend adding anything about parental notification in the definition of truancy between lines 139 and 142? 139. On the Red Library. Mm-hmm. I'm saying this just because when you defined truancy for us, you had mentioned that parents were unaware. There's nothing in the statement that is-

So when we have a student who hasn't shown up to school, we keep them as truant until we contact the family. And then once we contact the family, we're working with them to figure out what's going on. So then it changes from a truancy absence to an unexcused absence, which still triggers our response the same way. So I don't think we need to change anything, but I'm going to look over at Mr. Madison and see if he's got any thoughts, and if he doesn't, that's okay, too.

But the question was about truancy and the definition we have in our policy. So Mr. Madison, if you are going to speak, please come to the microphone. So I'm going to read it to you because you don't have a copy unless Lori has a copy. Do you have a copy? Not yet. Oh, there you go. So it's just where we define the truancy as the parent is unaware or not supporting. And it just says that,

and I explained the definition of that, and that usually when we call home and the parent finds out their kid isn't in school, they aren't supporting of it, so we change it to an unexcused absence versus a truancy absence. But if there's any clarity you think we could add. Take a minute to look at the line here. Take your time.

Mm-hmm. And it does say, on line 141, "All cases of truancy shall be reported to the parents," and we do that really timely. Thank you. Yes, I don't believe that we need to add anything additionally because, as Ms. Evans indicated, the school is actively-- I mean, a lot of times, if a

particular student is truant, there's probably been some prior contact with the student. And also, we typically see truancy at the high school level. So often, you're right, parents may know when their kid is having some issues with attendance gaps. But in most cases, there's already some relationship. Most of the kids that are truant,

there's been some type of relationship established already, with the school-based attendance team. So I don't believe there's anything that we need to add in the policy. This is based on my experience. Thank you for the clarification. I don't have further questions. I was going to suggest for the committee

that we bring this back as action, noting there are some additional changes to be made at the next meeting. Is everyone in agreement with that? Okay, perfect. So with that, I believe there's nothing else. We'll move on to item 5.02, which is revised policy 5170 on substance abuse education, and Ms. Evans is also going to present this item.

This is a really small update, but a very important update. So we wanted to align with House Bill 1486 relating to public schools, including information about the addictive potential of time spent using certain electronic devices. So if you look at line 22, you'll see where we added this statement to educate students about time spent using electronic devices such as computers, cell phones, and other smart devices and the addictive potential

thereof, which aligns with the two items above. Committee members, is there any discussion on this item? Ms. Chandler? I'll just say I'm very heartened to see this change. I'm happy to see that the code's been updated.
